opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic issue is that our whole grantmaking apparatus was built for a world where the binding constraint is finding good people and good projects, not money. Historically, a program officer's job is to find a promising researcher or organization, spend weeks getting to know them, write up an investigation, get it approved, and then check in over a year or two. That process is fundamentally about evaluating humans and their judgment, and it scales with how many program officers you have. If you want to spend a lot more, you either hire a lot more grantmakers, which is slow, or you make bigger grants to the same small set of organizations.

But if you take seriously the idea that AI systems are getting good enough to do a meaningful fraction of the actual work, say a lot of empirical safety research, evals, literature synthesis, software engineering, then the picture flips. The bottleneck stops being "is there a talented team that can absorb this money?" and becomes "can we specify the task well, buy enough compute and inference, and verify the output is good?" That's a very different skill set. It looks more like procurement or managing a research pipeline than traditional philanthropy.

So to spend a billion dollars well on highly automatable work, you'd need to think about things we're not really set up for: how do you write task specs precise enough that you can farm them out at scale? How do you build evaluation and quality control so you're not paying for a mountain of plausible-looking junk? How do you move fast enough that the window when this work is most valuable, before transformative systems arrive, doesn't close while you're still in your normal approval cycle? And how do you decide between spending on compute directly versus funding the humans who orchestrate the AI?

I'd also add that the timing matters. If AI capabilities are improving quickly, then the same dollar buys much more useful work in a year or two than it does today, but there may also be a point where it's too late for that work to matter. Figuring out when to deploy money, rather than just whether a given grant is good, is a question our existing process mostly doesn't ask. So I think it really does call for a different mindset, not just a scaled-up version of what we already do.

r001.rationale: The response says program officers investigate grants and get them approved, and argues that the existing process is ill-suited to highly automatable work. It does not communicate that junior staff originate proposals for approval up the hierarchy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to notice is that the whole machinery of a place like Open Phil was built around a particular bottleneck, which is that grantmaking judgment is scarce and expensive. You have a relatively small number of program officers, each of whom has spent years building up a model of a field, and the process is designed to allocate their attention carefully. You investigate a grant, you write up a memo, it gets reviewed, there's a lot of back and forth, and the time cost of that is actually fine when you're moving tens of millions of dollars and each decision is sort of bespoke.

But if you imagine a world where a lot of the actual work, the literature reviews, the cost-effectiveness modeling, the drafting of proposals, even a big chunk of the evaluation of those proposals, can be done by AI systems at a tiny fraction of the cost, then the bottleneck shifts. It's no longer "we can only look at thirty things this year." It becomes "we can look at three thousand things, and now the question is how do we decide what to trust, how do we set the objectives, and how do we avoid just doing a lot of fast, mediocre work at scale."

And a billion dollars is a number where the old process just breaks. You can't have a human carefully reading every memo at that volume. So you need something more like a portfolio or an institutional design question. What are the things humans actually need to be in the loop on? What are the checks that catch systematic errors rather than one-off errors, because systematic errors are the ones that get amplified when you automate? How do you structure incentives for the people and the systems doing the work so that you're not just rewarding whatever looks good to the evaluator?

I also think there's a cultural piece. Organizations that are used to being careful and slow find it genuinely hard to say, "Okay, we're going to move much faster and tolerate more variance because the cost of a bad grant has gone down relative to the cost of missing a good one." That's a real shift in how you think about risk, and I don't think you get there just by adding tools to the existing workflow. You have to actually rethink what the process is for.

r001.rationale: The response says the existing bespoke, staff-intensive process breaks at billion-dollar scale, but it does not describe junior staff originating proposals for approval up the hierarchy.

astra-6.text:
Well, if the work is highly automatable, then the bottleneck might shift from doing the work to deciding what work is worth doing and evaluating whether it succeeded. And our grantmaking process is largely built around a world where human labor is scarce: you find a team you trust, assess their plans, and fund them to work for a few years.

If a billion dollars could instead buy an enormous amount of automated research, I don’t think you can assume that same process will scale. You might want to fund lots of small experiments, get results quickly, and then allocate much more money to the approaches that look promising. But that requires being able to evaluate the results quickly enough—and, for some of the things we care about, evaluation is really hard.

So I think the question is less, ‘Can we afford to produce all this work?’ and more, ‘Do we have a process that can turn all this additional capacity into outcomes we actually value?’

r001.rationale: The response says the existing grantmaking process may not scale to highly automatable work, but it does not communicate that junior staff originate proposals for approval up the hierarchy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key thing is that the process we use to make grants today is very dependent on human judgment and human attention. A program officer develops a view about an area, gets to know potential grantees, and makes a fairly detailed case for a grant. And that can make sense when you're funding a relatively small number of substantial projects.

But imagine that a billion dollars could buy an enormous amount of AI labor, and that you could deploy that labor on millions of different research tasks. You probably wouldn't want a program officer individually evaluating every one of those tasks. You'd want a process that can try lots of things, evaluate the results, and allocate more resources to the things that seem to be working.

So it's not just a question of taking our current grantmaking process and running it faster. It's a question of what decisions humans should still be making, what we can delegate, and how we get enough feedback to know whether the work is actually useful. We might need to spend much more effort designing that system up front, because the amount of work it could direct would be so large.

r001.rationale: The response says today’s grantmaking relies on program officers’ individual judgment and would not scale to millions of tasks. It does not mention junior staff originating proposals or proposals being approved up the hierarchy.
